content: Infectious salmon anemia (ISA) is a viral disease that primarily affects Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) and has caused significant losses in fish farms located in Canada, Norway, and Scotland. The causative agent of this disease is the infectious salmon anemia virus (ISAV), which is the sole species within the genus Isavirus, belonging to the family Orthomyxoviridae. Pathology As the name suggests, ISA leads to severe anemia in infected fish. Affected fish often exhibit pale gills and may swim near the water surface, gasping for air. However, the disease can also progress without any visible external signs of illness. In such cases, the fish may maintain a normal appetite but die suddenly. The disease can spread slowly across an infected farm, and in severe outbreaks, mortality rates can approach 100%. Post-mortem examinations of infected fish reveal a variety of pathological changes. The liver and spleen may appear swollen, congested, or partially necrotic. The circulatory system may fail, and the blood can become contaminated with dead blood cells. Red blood cells that remain are often fragile and prone to rupture, while the number of immature and damaged blood cells increases. ISA shares similarities with influenza viruses in terms of its characteristics. However, the exact mechanisms of transmission and the natural reservoirs of ISAV remain incompletely understood. In addition to Atlantic salmon, sea-run brown trout (Salmo trutta) and rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) can also be infected by the virus. These species, however, do not develop clinical disease, suggesting that they may act as carriers and reservoirs for ISAV. Spread of the Disease The first documented outbreak of ISA occurred in the autumn of 1984 among Atlantic salmon farmed along the southwest coast of Norway. The disease spread gradually, and by June 1988, it had become widespread and severe enough for the Norwegian Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Food to classify it as a notifiable disease. In the summer of 1996, a new disease emerged among farmed Atlantic salmon in New Brunswick, Canada, with high mortality rates. After extensive scientific investigation, this disease was identified as hemorrhagic kidney syndrome. Studies conducted by Norwegian and Canadian scientists conclusively demonstrated that the same virus was responsible for both ISA and hemorrhagic kidney syndrome. In May 1998, a salmon farm at Loch Nevis on the west coast of Scotland reported a suspected outbreak of ISA. This suspicion was confirmed, and by the end of the year, the disease had spread to an additional 15 farms, including those on the Scottish mainland, Skye, and Shetland. Transmission The transmission of ISAV occurs through direct contact with infected fish or their secretions. The virus can also spread via contaminated equipment or personnel who have handled infected fish. ISAV is capable of surviving in seawater, making proximity to an infected farm a significant risk factor for uninfected farms. Recent studies have shown that sea lice, small crustacean parasites that damage the protective mucous, scales, and skin of salmon, can carry the virus on their surface and within their digestive tract. However, the direct transmission of ISA via sea lice has not been conclusively demonstrated. It is also unclear whether ISAV can replicate within sea lice, as viruses are typically highly host-specific, unlike certain bacterial diseases that can replicate in arthropod vectors such as ticks. Control and Treatment ISA poses a major threat to the sustainability of salmon farming and is classified as a List One disease under the European Commission’s fish health regime. This classification mandates the complete eradication of all fish stocks on a farm where an outbreak is confirmed. The economic and social consequences of both the disease and the control measures are profound. ISA is also considered a serious threat to declining populations of wild salmon. Anecdotal evidence suggests that fish surviving an initial infection may develop immunity to the virus. Efforts are currently underway to develop a vaccine against ISA. Recent research indicates that the North American strain of ISAV may differ slightly from the Norwegian strain, making it unlikely that the disease’s emergence in Canada was due to the importation of infected Norwegian fish. This raises the possibility that a single vaccine may only be effective in specific regions and for a limited duration.
